items.title: Business secretary writes to Poundland owner as administration fears build
items.summary: Jonathan Reynolds has written to Gordon Brothers, which bought retailer for £1 last summer, to ‘establish the facts’ The business secretary has written to the owner of Poundland amid fears that the cut-price retailer could collapse into administration, threatening to overshadow John Healey’s budget. Sources said that Gordon Brothers, the US investment firm that bought the 600-store Poundland chain for £1 last summer, looks set to appoint administrators to the struggling retailer. Continue reading...
items.body:
The business secretary has written to the owner of Poundland amid fears that the cut-price retailer could collapse into administration, threatening to overshadow John Healey’s budget.
Sources said that Gordon Brothers, the US investment firm that bought the 600-store Poundland chain for £1 last summer, looks set to appoint administrators to the struggling retailer.
Jonathan Reynolds has written to Gordon Brothers to establish the latest situation at the company, which employs 12,000 staff.
The company rejected the only bid to take on the group – which includes the 50-store Dealz chain in Ireland – as a solvent company in its entirety, from Northern Ireland’s Martin Property Group, earlier this week.
It is understood Gordon Brothers is poised to file a notice of intention to appoint the advisory firm AlixPartners as administrator, potentially as early as Wednesday. Three independent directors appointed to help oversee a sale have quit amid disquiet over the move towards insolvency.
The timing of the move threatened to overshadow Healey’s first budget as chancellor, amid longstanding complaints from companies over costs imposed by the government on businesses.
Barry Williams, the boss of Poundland, wrote to workers saying the rejection of the bid from Martin Property Group was “unexpected, unwanted and wholly avoidable”.
An improved bid from the Northern Irish firm has not been ruled out.
However, sources said that Martin’s bid fell well short of Gordon Brothers’ hopes to recoup the £30m in debts it took on with Poundland. The bid is understood to be worth more than £15m, with only a portion upfront.
One industry source said that suppliers to Poundland were already beginning to hold back on deliveries, making it tougher for the group to secure a rescue bid.
Industry insiders said Gordon Brothers wanted to move quickly as Poundland was flush with stock ahead of the busy Christmas period. A quick break-up of the chain, with parcels of stores and stock sold off, would lead to a maximum return for the restructuring specialist, sources said.
“Gordon Brothers has a simple choice. It can accept an offer from Martin Group, worth at least half of the £30m which it secured for £1, or get significantly more than that by busting the business,” a source said. “The only thing that can change this is if they feel the moral or public relations duty.”
Reynolds has instructed his chief strategic business adviser, David Bickerton, to “establish the facts” regarding Poundland’s potential collapse, as first reported by the Financial Times. He is understood to have contacted Gordon Brothers but not Poundland’s management team, which had backed the Martin Property Group bid.
A business department spokesperson said: “We know this will be a concerning time for Poundland employees, their families and communities across the UK.
“This is a commercial process and ultimately a decision for Poundland’s owners, so it would not be appropriate for the government to comment further.”
Gordon Brothers is understood to believe that it can raise more cash – as much as £30m – and keep more jobs in place long-term by breaking up Poundland and selling off the stock and stores to a variety of retailers.
There could be as many as eight interested parties, including the US investment firm Fortress, which owns Poundstretcher, and the owner of The Range. B&M is thought to be interested in taking on at least some outlets.
However, one industry insider said: “Who is going to take on 600 high street stores?” He predicted that up to 500 could be left without a buyer in the event of a break-up, leading to significant job losses.
Gordon Brothers has been approached for comment.

items.title: Autumn Budget 2026: In defence of cheaper gherkins, nature’s Ozempic
items.summary: In today’s Autumn Budget 2026, Chancellor John Healey announced he would be suspending tariffs on 100 supermarket products, including the humble gherkin. Adam Bloodworth on his love for the humble pickled vegetable, which is both delightfully crunchy and a hack to health My housemate Will has always been the sort of man with impossible levels [...]
items.body:
Autumn Budget 2026: In defence of cheaper gherkins, nature’s Ozempic
In today’s Autumn Budget 2026, Chancellor John Healey announced he would be suspending tariffs on 100 supermarket products, including the humble gherkin. Adam Bloodworth on his love for the humble pickled vegetable, which is both delightfully crunchy and a hack to health
My housemate Will has always been the sort of man with impossible levels of fitness. So when I started a new eat-healthier regime, I went to Will with some questions. I didn’t ask how he got muscular (I assumed that would be from lifting weights) – what felt more relatable was to ask him what he was eating. One of the hacks, he said, is gherkins. They have three calories a piece, he told me, beaming, in our kitchen.
So it was music to my ears when Burnham’s first budget unveiled an unprecedented price-drop for gherkins in the form of a 12 per cent tariff cut for importing them. Speaking today, Chancellor John Healey announced he would be suspending tariffs on 100 supermarket products, including gherkins, to make them more affordable for all.
They also have tartness, a light sweetness, and that famously generous crunch. Once the whole gherkin is inserted into your mouth, they require you to eat a bit like a dog, jaw swinging, eyes fixed, to ensure that everything – juice, flesh – is contained. You could cut them in half but where’s the fun in that? These great, cumbersome things are a workout in themselves.
Autumn Budget 2026 and the return of the gherkin
Anyway, try eating a whole jar at once. That’s what I do, on the regular. It’s now it’s become a part of my personality.
There’s no denying that after demolishing a whole vessel, chewing a family’s week-long supply of the vinegary veg, I’m exhausted. As well as embarrassed. But it’s worth it in the end.
Polishing off a whole jar does something to your brain: all that chewing makes you feel like you’ve eaten lots. It’s nature’s Ozempic.
At this point I should make clear that it is important not to rely fully on gherkins (always consult your doctor etcetera, etcetera) but you can rely a little bit on them. The fact is I was over-eating and gherkins helped me face the mental block of that head-on, and half an hour after blasting through a jar I could more healthily assess the rest of the food I was going to have for dinner, and it would be far less than I would have had if I hadn’t already gobbed the gherkins.
Leathery bad boys
I’ve taken to buying tins of them to eat at my desk. Sometimes the CEO walks past midway through me crunching down on one of the leathery bad boys, the gherkin half sticking out of my mouth. What can you do? I guess this is just my life, now.
Anyway, I’ve managed to lose five or six kilograms and get within a good weight. It’s about to be party season and I’m sure I’ll crumble a bit at those events, where there will presumably not be a ready supply of pickled veg – but I’m sure I won’t crumble as much as I would have done in my pre-gherkin days.
But I don’t want this to just be about a hedonistic man trying to stay on the right side of the tracks. Nor do I want this to be about the Autumn Budget 2026, that great signifier of autumn and the cold. I want this to be about gherkins. Intensely flavourful, humorously shaped, cartoon like in their curvature, they are joyful little misfits, refreshing for the palette and for the soul. We haven’t even talked about cutting them up and putting them in sandwiches, which is such a popular way of eating them that Pret recently experienced a temporary, stressful shortage.
Indeed my biggest fear is that the new, lower-priced gherkins following the budget might lead to even more shortages. I’ll have to stock up.
Anyway, it’s time to stop writing about gherkins. I have a jar of them to eat before I decide what to have for lunch.

items.body:
Interbrand, the world’s leading brand consultancy, today released its annual Best Global Brands report, with this year’s luxury analysis highlighting a sector increasingly defined by consistency and resilience in an ever-challenging marketplace.
Reduced consumer spending and shifting market behaviours have created a demanding environment for brands within the sector. Despite this, the strongest luxury brands have demonstrated that disciplined brand management and unwavering desirability remain strong drivers of value creation.
Interbrand Best Global Brands 2026
Hermès emerges as the world’s most valuable luxury brand
Hermès (#15, BV: $45.2bn) stood out as a top performer in the category, increasing its Brand Value by 10.6%, overtaking Louis Vuitton (#16, BV: 45.1bn) for the first time. Throughout the year, emphasis on craftsmanship, controlled scarcity and expanding experiential initiatives such as ‘Hermès in the Making’ have contributed to this success and provided resilience in a shifting wider luxury market.
Chanel (#24, BV: $32.9bn) also delivered strong growth, rising 8.1%, maintaining its position amongst the world’s most powerful luxury brands – thanks to an important period of creative renewal under new Artistic Director Matthie Blazy, bringing fresh energy to the brand, whilst retaining the design codes and creative identity that have made the icon distinctive.
Jewellery brands continue to shine
Cartier (#69, BV: $12.2bn) and Tiffany & Co (#91, BV: $8.1bn) grew 9.4% and 6.2% respectively, demonstrating that the winners in luxury are those who have strengthened desirability rather than relying on existing scale. Both brands invested in creativity, cultural partnerships and elevated retail experiences, highlighting how consumers reward brands able to unite heritage and contemporary service.
Heritage alone is no longer enough
Louis Vuitton (#16, BV: 45.1bn), once the largest brand by value in the sector, declined by 6.9% to $45.1bn, despite major investment into partnerships and category expansion. Dior (#85, BV: $8.9bn) fell 5.0%, while Gucci (#93, BV: $8.1bn) saw the sharpest decline, with its brand value falling by 30.7%, resulting in a 24-place drop to #93. Despite efforts to reset its creative direction, the brand continued to struggle with significantly reduced desirability and weak performances in key markets. Prada (#96, BV: $7.6bn) also struggled, falling ten places to #96, after a 15.1% reduction in Brand Value.
The results showcase a growing challenge for brands in luxury – heritage remains valuable, but consumers expect brands to evolve culturally and creatively, while remaining authentic to the qualities that made them desirable in the first place.
What did the winners get right in 2026?
This year’s ranking suggests that luxury is entering a period of polarisation, where brands with exceptional desirability, coherence and authenticity can thrive, whilst others are finding that legacy and heritage no longer guarantee growth. Luxury is no longer about what a product does, but what a brand means.
Brands which create value through disciplined brand development surpass those who have relied on heritage, scale and momentum. Hermès showcased how effective positioning, scarcity, and emotional connection can reinforce brand strength and commercial performance, whereas Gucci’s decline demonstrated that even the most powerful brands must continue to earn relevance and maintain consumer desire.

items.title: Holland & Barrett expands Irish operations with €17.5m investment
items.summary: Discover what's happening in retail today, Retail Times publishes international & UK retail news covering products, data, tech, packaging, people, research, comment and much more. From 1 November 2026, fulfilment of Holland & Barrett’s Irish online orders will […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! items.body:
Holland & Barrett, the UK’s leading health and wellness retailer, has today announced a €17.5 million investment across digital and retail fulfilment in Ireland over the next three years, as it builds on its long-standing partnership with Kildare-based Road Truck Services (RTS).
From 1 November 2026, fulfilment of Holland & Barrett’s Irish online orders will move from the UK to Ireland through an expanded three-year partnership with RTS, building on an eight-year relationship spanning import, customs, warehousing and distribution. The move will see €8.2 million invested in a new digital fulfilment model, alongside €9.3 million relating to existing retail fulfilment operations with RTS, bringing the total investment to €17.5 million over the next three years.
As part of the move, around €1.5 million of additional stock will be held locally, bringing Holland & Barrett’s total Irish stockholding to approximately €4.7 million. Around 328,000 orders and 1.8 million units are expected to flow through the Irish logistics network each year.
The expanded partnership is also expected to support around 20 additional RTS roles, alongside agency support during peak periods and a further 6-10 indirect roles, with recruitment focused on Kildare town and surrounding areas.
For customers, the move will mean greater choices on online orders from 1 November, with the existing 5kg weight limit lifted and additional products from 34 Irish brands available online. Next-day delivery is planned to launch from 1 December.
The investment comes as Holland & Barrett continues to grow its presence in Ireland. Approximately 2.8 million customers shopped with the business over the past year, and it now operates 70 stores and employs 419 colleagues across the country.
Holland & Barrett has also reached the top 10 in the 2026 Irish Customer Experience Report and continues to invest in its Irish store estate, with 90% of the estate now modernised, including the recently opened 5,909 sq. ft. Galway store.
Vineta Bajaj, Group CFO at Holland & Barrett, said: “Ireland is one of our strongest-performing markets and an important part of Holland & Barrett’s growth story. We’re seeing real momentum across both stores and digital, and we want to build on that by continuing to invest in the people, infrastructure and partnerships that will support our ambitions in Ireland for the long term.
“Our relationship with RTS has grown over eight years, and this next step means we can bring even more of our Irish operation closer to our customers. Holding more stock locally will help us deliver faster and offer greater choice and availability, while allowing us to continue investing in Ireland and building our presence in what is a very important market for us.”
Mick McConnell, Managing Director, Road Truck Services, said: “We’re incredibly proud of our partnership with Holland & Barrett, which has gone from strength to strength over the past eight years. Growing together has enabled us to expand our warehousing and transport capabilities, strengthen our business and secure other high-profile contracts.
“This latest investment marks an exciting new chapter in our relationship, creating jobs locally and allowing us to play an even bigger role in supporting Holland & Barrett’s growth in Ireland.”

items.title: Fed reacts to new increase in National Living Wage
items.summary: The Federation of Independent Retailers (The Fed) has reacted to a reported increase in the National Living Wage, albeit at a slightly slower rate of increase than in recent years. The minimum wage paid to people in the UK aged 21 and over is expected… This story continues at Fed reacts to new increase in National Living Wage Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
The minimum wage paid to people in the UK aged 21 and over is expected to rise by 3.9%, from the current £12.71 to £13.20 an hour from April 2027, with the increase expected to be confirmed by the chancellor in today’s Budget.
Meanwhile, the minimum wage for those aged 18–21 is expected to rise by a similar rate of 3.9%, from £10.85 to £11.27 an hour.
However, this is a lower increase than the 16.3% and 8.5% rises for younger workers that took effect in April 2025 and April 2026 respectively.
The expected increases come at a time when the Office for National Statistics (ONS) records inflation at approximately 3.5% in the year to September.
Whilst independent retailers are major employers, the Fed has repeatedly raised concerns that sharp increases in the minimum wage, combined with higher National Insurance Contributions and other rising operating costs, are making it increasingly difficult for independent businesses to recruit and retain staff.
Hemanshu Patel, national president of the Fed, said: “Independent retailers want to pay their staff fairly, but the Government must recognise that every increase in employment costs has to be paid for by a business already facing significant financial pressures.
“For many independent retailers, these are not simply figures on a spreadsheet. They affect decisions about whether they can afford to take on new staff, offer hours to younger workers or maintain their existing workforce.
“We are concerned that, without proper consideration of the cumulative costs facing employers, the government risks making it harder for young people to find work and for independent retailers to continue providing jobs in their local communities.
“We want to see fair pay, but we also need a sustainable environment in which independent retailers can employ people, invest in their businesses and continue serving their communities.”
Chancellor set to increase minimum wage while pausing youth pay parity

items.body:
Witchmark, the multi-award-winning English distillery based in Wiltshire, has secured its largest retail distribution deal to date with Majestic Wine, less than two years after launching its first spirits at the end of 2024.
The rollout is set to cover 39 Majestic stores across the Southwest in the coming months, with the liquid currently stocked at 29, paving the way for a significantly stronger retail presence throughout the distillery’s heartland.
Witchmark’s Single Origin Vodka is a smooth and creamy, yet characterful spirit made from barley grown on the distillery’s Fonthill Estate. It is a multi-award- winning spirit, including a Gold Outstanding award at the IWSC with a score of 98 points. For the perfect serve at home, Witchmark recommends mixing with premium grapefruit soda for a hassle-free, delicious Paloma.
Meanwhile, Witchmark’s Black Lime Gin is a bold and adventurous spirit with a rich base of juniper and coriander, elevated with the dark, smoky tang of black lime and the numbing spice of Szechuan pepper, a gin for those who seek to explore something more unexpected. Witchmark say that this works very well in a G&T, but if you’re looking for something different, then look no further than the
Chilmark Stone. This serve combines 25ml of Black Lime Gin with 25ml of Sweet Vermouth and is topped with 50ml of Ginger Ale for a good low-ABV alternative, especially for those who like a stirred-down drink.
Jon Carson, commercial director at Witchmark Distillery, shared: “Securing a listing with Majestic is a major milestone for Witchmark and our largest retail distribution deal to date. Majestic has built an exceptional portfolio and is highly selective about the brands it supports, so we are incredibly proud to join its range as an emerging English spirits producer.
“This listing reflects the hard work of our entire team and the growing demand for distinctive, provenance-led English spirits. We’re excited to introduce our award-winning Single Origin English Vodka and Black Lime Gin to Majestic customers across the Southwest, and hopefully more widely in the future.”
“Witchmark Vodka has real character and quality as a spirit,” shared James Cox, Buyer at Majestic Wine. “Together with the distinctive Black Lime Gin, it gives our customers an exciting introduction to Witchmark and further enhances our growing offering of high-quality English spirits.”
Witchmark’s Single Origin Vodka and Black Lime Gin are available now from select Majestic stores. RRP £43.

Historic French wine house Calvet is taking its partnership with award-winning wine expert, author and broadcaster Helen McGinn into the supermarket aisle, launching a new on-pack campaign across seven wines available in over 2000 […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! items.body:
French wine brand launches ‘Carefully Selected by Helen McGinn’ neck tags across seven wines, bringing expert recommendations directly to supermarket shelves.
Historic French wine house Calvet is taking its partnership with award-winning wine expert, author and broadcaster Helen McGinn into the supermarket aisle, launching a new on-pack campaign across seven wines available in over 2000 stores across Tesco, Waitrose, Morrisons, Sainsbury’s as well as online with Ocado.
The new neck tags carry the message ‘Carefully Selected by Helen McGinn’, putting Helen’s personal recommendations directly in front of shoppers and helping them navigate the French wine category and choose their next bottle with confidence.
The launch marks the next phase of Calvet’s A Taste of France with Helen McGinn campaign, extending the partnership beyond digital content and into the retail environment, where shoppers are making their purchasing decisions.
Launched in April 2026, the partnership has seen Helen introduce consumers to French wines through a six-part Instagram series that combines regional discoveries with accessible recipes, seasonal food pairings, and practical wine advice.
Now, Calvet is bringing that expertise directly to supermarket shelves, creating a recognisable endorsement designed to encourage shoppers to explore French wines they might otherwise overlook.
For French wine, this addresses a familiar challenge in the UK off-trade. While many New World wines are labelled prominently by grape variety, French wines often lead with their region or appellation, making the category harder for less experienced shoppers to navigate.
By placing Helen’s recommendations directly on selected bottles, Calvet aims to simplify decision-making, build consumer confidence, and encourage discovery across its French wine portfolio.
Helen McGinn said: “There’s so much to love about French wine, but I know that standing in front of a supermarket shelf full of different regions and labels can sometimes feel a little overwhelming. That’s why I’m delighted to work with Calvet to put my recommendations directly on the bottles. Whether you’re looking for something to enjoy with dinner or simply fancy trying something new, I hope these little tags make choosing a French wine feel that bit easier.”
Seven French Wines, Carefully Selected by Helen McGinn
The new neck tags feature across seven wines from Calvet’s Prestige, Réserve and regional ranges, spanning Bordeaux, the Rhône and Loire:
• Calvet Prestige Bordeaux Merlot Cabernet Sauvignon
• Calvet Prestige Bordeaux Sauvignon Blanc Fumé
• Calvet Prestige Côtes du Rhône Villages
• Calvet Réserve Bordeaux Merlot Cabernet Sauvignon
• Calvet Réserve Bordeaux Sauvignon Blanc
• Calvet Muscadet
• Calvet Cuvée du Cap Sauvignon Blanc AOP Bordeaux
From classic Bordeaux reds to fresh, food-friendly French whites, the selection showcases the breadth of Calvet’s portfolio and offers shoppers an accessible starting point for exploring different French wine styles.
Regis Bezaut, Group Marketing Manager, Calvet said: “Our partnership with Helen is about making French wine more approachable and relevant to today’s consumers. Through A Taste of France, we’ve been inspiring people to discover different regions and styles through food and everyday occasions. Bringing Helen’s recommendations into supermarket aisles is a natural next step, connecting that inspiration with the moment of purchase and helping shoppers feel confident choosing a bottle of Calvet.”
Founded in Bordeaux in 1818, Calvet has more than 200 years of winemaking heritage and a portfolio spanning some of France’s most celebrated wine regions.
The new on-pack campaign forms part of Calvet’s wider UK consumer engagement activity, with A Taste of France with Helen McGinn continuing throughout 2026 and into 2027.

items.title: IGD: retailers face flat-volume Christmas as shoppers trade down on essentials and up on treats

More than half (51%) of shoppers say they plan to buy more premium own-label products, highlighting how consumers […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! items.body:
UK consumers will save on festive essentials while trading up to premium treats this Christmas, creating a more polarised festive basket and leaving grocery retailers facing modest value growth but largely flat volumes, according to IGD research.
More than half (51%) of shoppers say they plan to buy more premium own-label products, highlighting how consumers are increasingly seeking affordable indulgence despite ongoing pressure on household budgets.
Despite shopper confidence falling to -3 in September, Christmas spending is expected to remain resilient. Rather than cutting back across the board, IGD expects shoppers to make deliberate trade-offs, seeking savings on commodity categories before reinvesting in centrepieces, desserts, party food and drinks.
This trend is expected to create opportunities for both discounters and premium own-label ranges as shoppers save on everyday essentials while selectively trading up on festive treats.
Jon Wright, Head of Insight at IGD, said:
“Shoppers still want to create memorable festive occasions, but they’re becoming increasingly strategic about where they save and where they spend. The retailers that perform best will help shoppers make those trade-offs, combining strong value credentials with compelling opportunities to trade up.”
Home entertaining gains momentum
IGD also expects more festive spending to shift into the home as consumers look to reduce spending on restaurants, pubs and takeaways.
Rather than cancelling celebrations, many shoppers are expected to recreate them at home through premium meal solutions, party food and drinks. This is likely to create further opportunities for grocery retailers while increasing competitive pressure on parts of the hospitality sector.
Premium private-label ranges are expected to be among the biggest beneficiaries as consumers seek restaurant-quality experiences at home for less.
Retailers prepare for more unpredictable festive demand
IGD also expects promotions, loyalty schemes and early festive purchases to play a major role in Christmas 2026, with promotions accounting for 33.3% of December 2025 sales, the highest level since Christmas 2019.
Combined with growing demand for premium private-label products and at-home entertaining, pressure on household budgets could encourage shoppers to spread the cost of Christmas over a longer period, bringing festive spending forward and creating more uneven demand patterns across categories and channels.
IGD says retailers and suppliers will need to remain agile, ensuring strong availability across both value and premium festive lines while responding quickly to shifts in demand.
These findings are taken from IGD’s ‘Seven predictions for Christmas 2026’ retail analysis, available free as part of IGD’s Golden Quarter Christmas insights coverage.

items.title: What the growth of digital gaming means for online retail
items.summary: Discover what's happening in retail today, Retail Times publishes international & UK retail news covering products, data, tech, packaging, people, research, comment and much more. Britain’s video games market reached £8.76 billion in 2025, according to trade body Ukie’s annual consumer valuation. Spending increased by 7.4 per cent, with growth across software, hardware and the surrounding market for gaming culture. For retailers, the detail is more useful than the headline. Digital console spending rose by 9.2 per cent to £2.49 […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
Britain’s video games market reached £8.76 billion in 2025, according to trade body Ukie’s annual consumer valuation. Spending increased by 7.4 per cent, with growth across software, hardware and the surrounding market for gaming culture.
For retailers, the detail is more useful than the headline. Digital console spending rose by 9.2 per cent to £2.49 billion, while mobile spending increased by 7.9 per cent to £2.07 billion. Boxed software, by comparison, slipped by 1 per cent to £319 million.
Those figures describe a market in which the relationship with a customer increasingly continues after the initial purchase. Games can be downloaded, expanded, subscribed to and played across successive updates. The commercial challenge is keeping the entire experience understandable, including what customers own, what they can access and what they are paying for.
Growth does not follow one business model
“Online gaming” is often used as a broad description, but it contains businesses with different products and revenue models.
A full-price game involves an initial purchase. A subscription provides access under continuing terms, while a free-to-play title may earn revenue through optional purchases. Hardware and accessories add another layer, with spending that depends partly on release cycles and the equipment customers already own.
These distinctions matter when interpreting market growth. Rising revenue does not necessarily mean more people are buying complete games. Existing players may be spending differently, or a new console may be encouraging purchases elsewhere in the market.
For a retailer considering its own digital offering, the useful question is which part of that relationship it can support effectively. Selling a download code requires different information and customer service from selling a physical controller.
Casino gaming has its own commercial requirements
Adult casino gaming is another part of digital entertainment, with a different transaction structure from buying a game or paying for a subscription. An online casino gives customers access to individual games through an account, making the explanation of deposits, stakes and withdrawals an important part of the service.
Its market figures also require separate treatment. The Gambling Commission reported £8.3 billion in gross gambling yield for Great Britain’s remote casino, betting and bingo sector during April 2025 to March 2026, an increase of 6.9 per cent.
Gross gambling yield is not the same measure as consumer spending on video games. It broadly reflects stakes received less winnings paid out. Adding the two sectors’ headline figures together would therefore produce a misleading picture.
The useful business comparison concerns how digital services communicate transactions and access, rather than treating their revenues or products as interchangeable.
The product page now has to explain access
Physical products usually give customers a familiar reference point. A box arrives, the contents can be checked and ownership is relatively easy to understand.
Digital products introduce more questions. A purchase may require a particular platform account, compatible hardware or an existing base game. An expansion can look like a complete product to someone unfamiliar with the title.
These details belong near the purchase decision. Leaving them in a long description or a separate support page increases the chance of a misunderstanding.
A useful listing should make clear what is included and what is required. If access depends on a subscription, that should be apparent before payment. If a code is restricted to a region or platform, the customer needs that information while comparing products.
Retailers already recognise the value of accurate sizing and compatibility information. Digital entertainment requires the same discipline, applied to accounts, licences and access conditions.
Repeat spending creates a service obligation
A business built around ongoing access needs to maintain the relationship after checkout.
That includes reliable account access, clear renewal information and straightforward explanations when a product changes. A customer who paid once may need occasional help. A subscriber may need to understand a continuing sequence of payments and benefits.
The risk is assuming that a completed transaction proves the experience worked. A successful payment does not tell the retailer if the customer redeemed a code, accessed the content or understood what would happen next.
Support enquiries can reveal those gaps. Repeated questions about activation suggest a communication problem. Confusion about an expansion may indicate that the listing does not distinguish it clearly enough from the main game.
Resolving those issues can be more useful than adding another promotional message. It improves the purchase experience for customers who have already decided to spend.
Discovery needs more than a large catalogue
Digital distribution makes it possible to display an enormous selection without maintaining equivalent shelf space. That does not automatically make the selection easy to shop.
A customer searching for a cooperative game may care about local multiplayer, online play or the number of people supported. A parent buying a gift may need to understand age ratings and platform compatibility. An experienced player may want to exclude content they already own.
Filters and descriptions should reflect those different tasks. A long list ranked only by popularity leaves customers to investigate essential details themselves.
The same applies to recommendations. Suggesting an expansion without establishing that the customer owns the base game may create confusion rather than a useful additional sale.
Catalogue size has value when customers can navigate it confidently. Otherwise, a larger selection can simply mean more work before buying.
Physical retail still has a role
Digital software growth does not remove the opportunity for physical retailers. Ukie valued UK games hardware spending at £2.17 billion in 2025, with console and PC hardware both increasing.
The opportunity lies partly in helping customers assemble a working setup. Compatibility advice, demonstrations and informed staff can answer questions that product specifications leave unresolved.
There is also room to connect physical and digital purchases thoughtfully. Someone buying a console may need an explanation of subscriptions, storage and account setup before they need a list of additional products.
The growth of gaming gives retailers several possible routes, but each depends on understanding the purchase being made. A hardware sale, a digital licence and recurring access create different obligations. Businesses that explain those differences clearly give customers a better basis for choosing, and fewer reasons to contact support afterwards.

items.title: ACS tells committee of MPs about impact of rising costs on local shops
items.summary: Ahead of today’s Budget, the Association of Convenience Stores (ACS) has told an influential committee of MPs that the cost of trading is having an impact on retailers' ability to invest in their people and their businesses. ACS chief executive Ed Woodall gave evidence to… This story continues at ACS tells committee of MPs about impact of rising costs on local shops Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
ACS chief executive Ed Woodall gave evidence to the Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (BIST) Committee on entrepreneurship and business today in parliament yesterday (27 October), highlighting the rising cost of employment, business rates and energy in the convenience sector and the consequences of those increases.
Speaking during the evidence session, Woodall said: “We employ over 456,000 people in our sector, but while the number of people employed has stayed the same, the cost of wages has gone up, meaning that we’re increasingly paying for fewer hours.
“What this means is that retailers are taking on more hours in the shop themselves and they’re unable to work on the business, making it more difficult to turn a profit at the end of the year.”
The BIST committee inquiry is examining how people start and scale up businesses, and the barriers to business growth.
During the session, ACS told MPs that the most pressing thing retailers need to hear at the Budget is action on business rates.
Woodall continued: “Business rates have gone up by 79% as a sector since 2024 because more retailers have been dragged into paying rates. We need to see the Chancellor move the point at which businesses start paying rates from £12,000 rateable value to £18,000 rateable value so that no small shop owner pays rates.”

items.title: More than eight in ten Brits fear rising prices, poll shows
items.summary: More than eight in ten Brits are concerned about rising food prices (83%) and inflation (82%) ahead of today’s (28 October) Budget, according to new Opinium polling of over 2,000 UK adults commissioned by the British Retail Consortium (BRC). BRC’s latest Shop Price Monitor, showing… This story continues at More than eight in ten Brits fear rising prices, poll shows Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
BRC’s latest Shop Price Monitor, showing a 2.1% rise in shop price inflation for October, the highest since February 2024, appears to reflect those fears. The data also showed food prices up 2.9% over the year.
Retailers are doing everything they can to absorb costs and keep prices as low as possible for customers, but rising taxes have made this all but impossible.
The retail industry is facing £41bn in business taxes for 2026/27, a 20% increase in just two years.
Compared with other major economic sectors of the economy, retail, along with hospitality, has the highest effective tax rate, with nearly £3 paid in tax for every £4 of profit (72%). This compares to the financial sector, where the effective tax rate is less than £2 tax for every £4 profit (41%).
Retailers want chancellor Healey to support families by finding ways to reduce business costs and balance them more fairly across the economy.
Given the central role of retail in the affordability of food and other essentials, any move to increase taxes on retail businesses would inevitably push prices even higher for households.
Without action, business rates will rise by 3.5% in April 2027, in line with the September Consumer Price Index.
For retail, which already pays one fifth of the UK business rates, this increase would add approximately another £250m to costs.
BRC said today’s Budget offers a real opportunity to deliver jobs and improve living standards for households everywhere.
Giving retailers more breathing room on costs would allow more money to be directed to keeping prices down, while also helping the industry to create more opportunities for young people, at a time when there are nearly one million youth NEETs.
The BRC and its members are calling on the chancellor to raise the employer National Insurance threshold from £5,000 to £6,000, freeze the CPI-linked increase in business rates, and exempt retail premises from the high-value multiplier.
Helen Dickinson, chief executive of the British Retail Consortium, said: “The message from the public is clear: the cost of living remains a top concern. Households, retailers and the Government share a common aim of easing pressure on family finances and fixing the youth employment crisis. The Budget must deliver on both.
“To support this, the chancellor must address the barrage of costs and taxes currently raining down on the industry.
“Chief among these are business rates, which are set to rise by another £250m for retailers next April, and employer NICs, which are up by over £2bn in the last two years. Every pound spent on taxes and regulation is a pound not spent on keeping prices low for consumers.
“Action on business rates and NICs would go a long way to helping retailers deliver even better value for households and more jobs for young people. A Budget for shops and shoppers is also a Budget for communities everywhere.”

items.title: Government to probe Poundland crisis as unions warn of job losses 'before Christmas'
items.summary: Ministers are asking questions of the retailer's private equity owners, which have been the source of outrage as it looks increasingly likely that the business will be split up.
items.body:
Government to probe Poundland crisis as unions warn of job losses 'before Christmas'
The Government is now asking questions about the deepening crisis at Poundland - as up to 12,000 jobs are on the line, including in the Prime Minister's constituency.
Ministers are questioning the retailer’s private equity owners, Gordon Brothers, which have been the source of outrage as it looks increasingly likely that the business will be split up and sold.
Business secretary Jonathan Reynolds has instructed his chief strategic business adviser David Bickerton to ‘establish the facts’ over a potential collapse, the Financial Times reported.
And shop workers’ union Usdaw are set to meet with the minister for the future of work, Kate Dearden, today amid warnings of what would be the biggest High Street collapse in years.
Three directors, appointed less than a fortnight ago, last night walked out following a dramatic dispute with owners Gordon Brothers.
Government ministers are growing concerned as fears over a collapse of Poundland deepen
And the retailer’s own management last night hit out at the owners, calling the process ‘unexpected, unwanted and avoidable’.
The shake-up came after the owners, who bought Poundland for just €1 last year, turned down a rescue offer from would-be buyer Martin Property Group.
It is feared they will instead break the company up and sell off the shops piecemeal – or even let it fall into insolvency.
Speaking on Radio 4’s Today programme, Usdaw national officer Bally Auluk warned that thousands of employees ‘are potentially going to be put out of a job before Christmas in the coming days.’
The union, alongside the retailer’s management, wants to see the company stick with a bid from Irish company Martin Property Group, rather than selling off shops as piecemeal.
When asked if selling off shops in parts to multiplier bidders could actually be the best deal on the table, Auluk said: ‘You’re talking a minimal number of units that they're looking to sell.’
He added: ‘There’s no reason why they can't accept this fully funded bid from the Martin Property Group, which would have ensured the viability of the company going forward.’
But Gordon Brothers have said they are considering other bidders, after their talks with the Irish group broke down as they did not want to commit to a £30 million upfront payment.
Job losses could hit 600 shops and a distribution centre in Makerfield, Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s constituency.
Government adviser Bickerton is set to ask ‘fairly basic questions of senior people around Poundland’ in order to ‘establish what the situation is,’ the Financial Times reported.
A business department spokesman said: ‘We know this will be a concerning time for Poundland employees, their families and communities across the UK.
‘This is a commercial process and ultimately a decision for Poundland’s owners, so it would not be appropriate for the government to comment further.’

items.title: I gave Selfridges my vintage Chanel handbag to repair... but was sent back a cheap washbag: SALLY SORTS IT
items.summary: I took my vintage Chanel handbag to Selfridges for repair at The Handbag Clinic, which operates as a concession within the store, and paid £125.
items.body:
I gave Selfridges my vintage Chanel handbag to repair... but was sent back a cheap washbag: SALLY SORTS IT
I took my vintage Chanel handbag to Selfridges for repair at The Handbag Clinic, which operates as a concession within the store, and paid £125.
More than three months later, a parcel was delivered by a courier arranged by the firm.
Rather than my repaired bag, which I estimate is worth in excess of £7,000, it contained a Juicy Couture wash bag.
Despite extensive communication with The Handbag Clinic and Selfridges, both have effectively closed the case and placed responsibility on the courier, telling me that I must pursue the matter with it directly. Please help. A.F., Putney, west London.
Sally Hamilton replies: You told me you have been a loyal customer of the famous London department store for more than 60 years, so you were sorely disappointed by how matters were handled when your bag vanished.
You believe that somewhere between The Handbag Clinic and your home, the package was intercepted and your much-loved and expensive bag was stolen and replaced with the low-value wash bag.
Although upset, you felt confident Selfridges would step in and resolve the issue.
A reader was shocked when Selfridges sent her a cheap Juice Couture washbag in place of the expensive vintage Chanel Washbag she had put in for repair
You enlisted your two daughters to help as they are more tech-savvy in dealing with businesses online.
Despite their best efforts, they did not get very far. Both operations denied responsibility, saying the bag had left the repair workshop in the correct packaging and that CCTV footage proved it.
They said delivery images showed just a small tear in the package, consistent with normal wear and tear in transit rather than evidence of tampering.
Eventually, you were told you needed to take up your case with the courier.
This was incorrect advice. Under Section 29 of the Consumer Rights Act 2015, goods remain at the retailer’s risk until they are in the hands of the consumer. Only if shoppers organise a courier themselves do they take on that risk, and need to deal directly with the delivery firm if something goes awry.
I pointed this out to Selfridges, which hosts The Handbag Clinic on its premises, and asked for it to reopen your case in the hope of reaching a more satisfactory result.
Selfridges liaised with The Handbag Clinic, and the earlier investigations were reviewed.
The same conclusion was reached: The Handbag Clinic said it wasn’t responsible. However, on my intervention and recognising the upset, The Handbag Clinic decided to compensate you as a goodwill gesture.
The Handbag Clinic appeared to put considerable effort into working out what your lost bag – a 1980s vintage lambskin with tortoiseshell resin strap embellishments – might have been worth.
It compared sold prices across the pre-owned luxury bags market and enlisted the help of in-house specialists as well as an external expert.
It also trawled its database for evidence of a Juicy Couture wash bag, in case there had been a mix-up, but concluded there had never been such a bag on its premises. The upshot was an offer of £2,500 plus a refund of the £125 repair bill.
You were disappointed by this sum, saying you’d seen other comparable second-hand bags for sale online for as much as £7,000. Similar new versions cost £9,000.
I suspect that sellers’ asking prices for second-hand items are not the best guide, with sold values – the prices people have actually paid – more realistic.
So I could feel comfortable the offer to you was fair, I tracked down an expert myself.
I sent a photo and explanation of your bag’s age and provenance to Chiswick Auctions in west London. Popsy Kundi, head of designer handbags and fashion, responded swiftly, saying she believed £7,000 was ‘overstated’.
She added: ‘In my professional opinion, as it is not the classic flap style of Chanel bag, the estimated auction value would be in the region of £1,200-£2,200.’
The sum on the table, therefore, seemed realistic and fair. When I informed you of my findings, you were reassured, thanked me for my help and have now accepted the firm’s offer.
Can't access late husbands civil service pension
My husband died on March 19 and I haven’t received a penny from his civil service pension since May 16.
I’m 82, deaf, have atrial fibrillation and severe osteoporosis, and I live on my own.
Three more months have passed and still nothing has been received. I have car and house insurance to pay this month. Please help.
Name and address supplied.
Sally Hamilton replies: You are one of thousands of people caught up in the chaos that has engulfed the Civil Service Pension Scheme in 2026.
I have heard similar stories from several other readers facing huge delays in getting their pension paid.
Capita, the administrator of the scheme since December 2025 after inheriting it from MyCSP, is continuing to struggle with a huge backlog of cases and its own failure to hit service standard levels.
This may explain why you hadn’t received your rightful widow’s pension, but such an excuse doesn’t pay the bills.
With £7,000 spent on your husband’s funeral and large household costs to meet, the need for your pension income has become urgent.
Under the terms of your late husband’s pension, you were in line to receive his monthly payment in full for 91 days, then a reduced pension of 45 per cent thereafter.
Despite complying with all the demands from the administrators, including posting the death and marriage certificates and other papers within two weeks, the payments dried up after May.
By the time you wrote to me, 14 weeks had passed and you described being left without this money as ‘extremely cruel’. I agree.
When the extent of the administrative problems emerged earlier this year, Capita promised that bereavement cases would take priority.
So why were you still waiting? I asked Capita to pull its finger out. It spent about a week investigating, at which point it told me it had now issued your ‘finalisation letter’. This is the paperwork setting out the sums you will receive.
When we caught up, you were relieved to have your backdated pension finally in your account, even if it was four months late.
- Write to Sally Hamilton at Sally Sorts It, Money Mail, Northcliffe House, 2 Derry Street, London W8 5TT or email sally@dailymail.co.uk include phone number, address and a note addressed to the offending organisation giving them permission to talk to Sally Hamilton. items.title: Morrisons bins Instacart AI powered Caper Carts trial amid DoorDash acquisition talks
items.summary: In July, we reported that Morrisons had launched Instacart’s Caper Cart smart trolleys at a Preston supermarket, marking North American firm Instacart’s first retail partnership in the UK for its AI powered solution. Three months later, however, the retailer is pulling the trial as DoorDash enters i
items.body:
In July, we reported that Morrisons had launched Instacart’s Caper Cart smart trolleys at a Preston supermarket, marking North American firm Instacart’s first retail partnership in the UK for its AI powered solution.
Three months later, however, the retailer is pulling the trial as DoorDash enters into talks to acquire Instacart in a deal that could value the grocery technology specialist at around $17 billion. Separately, the latter said in a regulatory filing on Monday that it would wind down its Caper Cart business by the end of the second quarter of 2027, expecting pre-tax charges of $55 million to $80 million related to the move.
The plan is to reinvest any savings into strategic growth initiatives, which includes other in-store solutions like smart price tags and computer vision technology to help grocers track in-store inventory.
"Our customers are at the heart of everything we do, and we're always looking for ways to make their weekly shop easier, more rewarding, and more enjoyable, to give them more reasons to shop at Morrisons," Gordon Macpherson, Productivity Director at Morrisons, said during the launch of the trial.
“Caper smart trolleys do exactly that, giving customers real-time visibility of their spending, instant access to their More Card savings, and a more seamless experience in the aisle. We're proud to be the first UK retailer to bring this technology to our customers, and we look forward to seeing how shoppers in Preston and across Lancashire respond to this innovative new trolley in this in-store trial.”
Responding to the news, retail analyst Steve Dresser said on LinkedIn: "Not one to mock innovation, it's vital. But this was always overplayed and seemed to be a chance for people to get their name in lights, rather than a meaningful trial to scale."
A Morrisons spokesperson told RTIH: "We note that Instacart has announced a strategic decision to wind down its Caper Cart business. Our single store trial is due to complete shortly as planned and we’ll continue to test and learn until the end of the trial period. The trial has given us greater insight into the continued evolution of our customers shopping habits and we will continue to pilot and develop solutions to meet those needs."
And the winners are...
Morrisons is among the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards finalists.
Our winners will be revealed at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony, taking place at The HAC in Central London on Wednesday, 4th November.

The event will consist of a drinks reception, three course meal, awards ceremony presided over by award winning stand-up comedian, presenter, actor and broadcaster, Aurie Styla, and after party until 1am.

items.title: NI property group ‘exits from Poundland deal’
What to expect from John Healey’s first budget: who wins, who pays?
items.summary: Struggling households, new homebuyers and small shops stand to gain, while banks and online marketplaces could face higher levies You be the chancellor: play our budget game to see if you can balance the books John Healey will present his first budget on Wednesday, which will set the tone for Andy Burnham’s premiership. Despite the chancellor’s promises in the summer that the tax and spending event would not be beset by the leaks that preceded those of his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, both official and unofficial sources have indicated much of what Healey is likely to announce. Here’s what to expect: Continue reading...
items.body:
John Healey will present his first budget on Wednesday, which will set the tone for Andy Burnham’s premiership.
Despite the chancellor’s promises in the summer that the tax and spending event would not be beset by the leaks that preceded those of his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, both official and unofficial sources have indicated much of what Healey is likely to announce. Here’s what to expect:
How much money is there?
Healey will allocate about £1.42tn this year on day-to-day spending and public investment. About £100bn of this will go on debt interest after a rise in the interest rate the government pays to multidecade highs.
Most of this increase can be blamed on the Gulf conflict launched by the US and Israel at the end of February, which has taken the oil price to above $110 a barrel and the price of gas to levels not seen since late 2022.
Government borrowing in this financial year has fallen compared with 2025-26, but not by as much as the Office for Budget Responsibility estimated in March, mainly owing to higher debt financing. Healey is spending about £1bn a month more than forecast.
Those costs mean the buffer of £24bn built up in the last tax-raising budget is likely to have halved to £12bn, according to the Resolution Foundation thinktank. The Treasury would be more comfortable having this headroom at about £15bn, according to economists at ING.
It’s a headache the chancellor could do without when he needs extra cash to fund cost of living measures, but also higher defence spending and the prime minister’s pet projects, such as devolution.
What does he want to spend money on?
The chancellor has promised to give consumers and businesses “breathing space” with a range of measures to help with soaring costs.
Everyday fixes: This is what the Treasury calls its proposals to help struggling households. They include an extension of parental pay to more than 150,000 additional parents per year worth £388, covering self-employed fathers and partners who have previously missed out.
Healey will also end the carer’s allowance cliff-edge, so unpaid carers no longer lose more than their allowance once they hit their weekly earnings limit. He will also remove import tariffs on more than 100 products, including baked beans, chocolate and gherkins, to reduce their shop prices.
Energy bills: The chancellor is planning to spend more than £1bn to help poorer households struggling with soaring gas and electricity bills, with the bulk going towards an expansion of the existing Warm Home Discount. An additional £100 could be added to this £150 means-tested yearly rebate, funded by taxes rather than billpayers as the current discount is.
Burnham has already suspended VAT on electricity bills for six months and on Wednesday morning Healey announced he was scrapping standing charges on gas bills in a move he claimed would save 60% of households on average £45 a year.
Help for first-time homebuyers: The budget will provide more detail of how the “your first home” scheme – first announced at Labour’s annual party conference last month – will work in practice. The revamped version of the Tories’ “help to buy” programme will give first-time buyers a 20% equity loan towards a new-build home, with an initial interest-free period and a minimum deposit of just 2.5%.
Defence: Healey aims to plug a £4.7bn gap in the government’s defence investment plan, inherited from Keir Starmer, with cuts to other departmental budgets ikely to be the main source of funding. However, despite resigning in June over raising defence spending to 3% of GDP, a roadmap showing how that target will be hit by 2030 will now not come until the spending review next year.
What taxes could Healey raise?
Healey is unable to increase rates of income tax, national insurance, and VAT without breaking manifesto commitments and has promised to stick to Reeves’s fiscal rules and not borrow to fund day-to-day spending. However, these are some of the revenue-raising measures he’s reportedly considering.
Bank tax: The Guardian revealed this month that the budget’s main revenue-raising measure is expected to be a levy on banks. The sector’s resistance has been undermined by a run of bumper quarterly profits on the back of higher interest rates, culminating in HSBC revealing on Tuesday that its had risen 32% to about £7.2bn.
Jeremy Hunt cut the bank surcharge – a supplement to corporation tax – from 8% to 3% ahead of the last election and one option on the table is reversing this cut to raise more than £2bn a year.
Taxes on online sellers: There has been strong lobbying from Labour backbenchers and unions to increase the taxes paid by online marketplaces such as Amazon and eBay. The former Burnham adviser Andy Haldane used a Guardian interview to urge Healey to “level the playing field” with physical stores. One proposal reportedly drawn up would raise up to an extra £1bn by forcing them to collect VAT on behalf of large-scale sellers based in the UK as well as those overseas.
That money could be used to fund a cut in business rates paid by small high-street shops, possibly in the form of an increase to the threshold at which they start paying from £12,000 to £18,000. This would help the “bloody-minded entrepreneurs” that Healey has said he wants to support.
Other taxes: Alcohol duty is likely to rise in line with the retail prices index (RPI) measure of inflation, which will increase the tax on a pint from 50p to 52p.
What taxes is he expected not to touch?
Mansion tax: Treasury officials have played down speculation of significant changes to Reeves’s measure, which imposes an annual charge worth up to £7,500 on properties valued at more than £2m from April 2028. The chancellor was understood to be considering lowering the threshold to £1.5m, but London MPs have pushed back and are confident Healey has ruled out the move.
Capital gains tax: The chancellor has rejected calls by senior Labour MPs to raise CGT to the same levels as income tax. Some of his cabinet colleagues have called for the tax rates on income and asset gains to be equalised. However, influential figures, such as the former Treasury minister Jim O’Neill have pushed back, saying it would harm the incentives for wealth creators.
Fuel duty A longstanding freeze in fuel duty had already been extended to the end of the year, but it is due to rise by 3p a litre in January and 2p a litre in March. The default is also for an increase in line with RPI from April. However, with petrol and diesel at near-record highs the chancellor is expected to continue the freeze. Extending for an additional year could cost up to £2.7bn, according to the Institute for Fiscal Studies, while keeping it to 2029-30 would cost another £4bn.
Inheritance tax: While the Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch has proposed raising the tax-free threshold from £325,000 to £500,000 and excluding family homes from the calculation, Labour is not expected to propose any changes of its own.
Other measures
Devolution: Spreading decision-making to the far reaches of England is a major element of Burnham’s plans for economic growth. Healey will offer a £150m funding boost to help mayoralties and local authorities scale up for the new work they will carry out.
In addition there will be a £1.5bn borrowing facility. The package will also include the allocation of an initial £285m “good growth” funding next year, to be spent on local leaders’ priorities – which could include housing, transport links or high street regeneration.
Golden visas: Healey is understood to have scrapped plans for a new visa route to the UK aimed at wealthy people from overseas that were explored by the Treasury earlier in the year.

items.title: Amazon and Tiktok accused of dodging MP scrutiny over online shopping safety
items.summary: Amazon and Tiktok have been accused of dodging parliamentary scrutiny over consumer safety, after MPs raised concerns about the tech giants’ reluctance to appear before a committee hearing next week. Liam Byrne, chair of the Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (BIST) Committee, wrote to senior executives at both companies on Tuesday, warning that their unwillingness [...]
items.body:
Amazon and Tiktok accused of dodging MP scrutiny over online shopping safety
Amazon and Tiktok have been accused of dodging parliamentary scrutiny over consumer safety, after MPs raised concerns about the tech giants’ reluctance to appear before a committee hearing next week.
Liam Byrne, chair of the Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (BIST) Committee, wrote to senior executives at both companies on Tuesday, warning that their unwillingness to face questions risked undermining protections for British shoppers.
In letters addressed to Amazon’s UK director of public policy and Tiktok’s director of public policy for Northern Europe, Alistair Law, Byrne urged both firms to send representatives to the hearing on 3 November.
The session will look into consumer protections relating to the regulation of online marketplaces and products sold through them.
“Disregard of parliamentary oversight reflects badly on your company’s willingness to engage with policymakers, and hampers the committee’s ability to ensure regulation and protections are fit for purpose”, Byrne wrote.
“These protections are essential safeguards for the customers from whom you draw revenue”.
Amazon has offered written evidence instead of selecting one witness to speak across all topics, City AM understands, and has already given evidence to the committee twice in the past few years.
Ministers tighten online shopping rules
Earlier this year, the government launched proposals to hold online platforms to the same product safety standards as traditional retailers, following concerns about dangerous goods sold online, including lithium-ion batteries linked to fires.
The Law Commission has also proposed extending product liability rules to online marketplaces where defective goods are sold by businesses without an identifiable UK presence.
Such changes could leave platforms including Amazon liable for certain harms caused by products sold through third-party sellers.
The parliamentary row comes ahead of John Healey’s first Budget, amid reports that the Treasury is preparing a separate crackdown on VAT avoidance through online marketplaces.
Under the reported plans, platforms could be made responsible for collecting VAT from sellers with annual turnover exceeding £90,000, potentially raising up to £1bn for the Treasury.
Amazon has previously welcomed proposals to close the loophole, arguing that the changes would simplify compliance for legitimate sellers.
Byrne said the companies played a major role in the market and stressed the “vital importance of parliamentary scrutiny” concerning the safety and financial interests of UK consumers.
Both companies have been asked to make representatives available for next Tuesday’s hearing.

items.title: Holland & Barrett announces €17.5 million investment across digital and retail fulfilment in Ireland
items.summary: UK health and wellness retailer, Holland and Barrett, has announced a €17.5 million investment across digital and retail fulfilment in Ireland over the next three years.From 1st November, fulfilment of its Irish online orders will move from the UK to Ireland through an expanded three-year partnershi
items.body:
UK health and wellness retailer, Holland and Barrett, has announced a €17.5 million investment across digital and retail fulfilment in Ireland over the next three years.
From 1st November, fulfilment of its Irish online orders will move from the UK to Ireland through an expanded three-year partnership with Kildare-based Road Truck Services (RTS), building on an eight-year relationship spanning import, customs, warehousing and distribution.
The move will see €8.2 million invested in a new digital fulfilment model, alongside €9.3 million relating to existing retail fulfilment operations with RTS, bringing the total investment to €17.5 million over the next three years.
Around €1.5 million of additional stock will be held locally, bringing Holland & Barrett’s total Irish stockholding to approximately €4.7 million. Around 328,000 orders and 1.8 million units are expected to flow through the Irish logistics network each year.
The expanded partnership is also expected to support around 20 additional RTS roles, alongside agency support during peak periods and a further 6-10 indirect roles, with recruitment focused on Kildare town and surrounding areas.
For customers, the move will mean greater choices on online orders from 1st November, with the existing 5kg weight limit lifted and additional products from 34 Irish brands available online. Next-day delivery is planned to launch from 1st December.
The investment comes as Holland & Barrett grows its presence in Ireland. Approximately 2.8 million customers shopped with the business over the past year, and it now operates 70 stores and employs 419 colleagues across the country.
Vineta Bajaj, Group CFO at Holland & Barrett, says: “Ireland is one of our strongest performing markets and an important part of Holland & Barrett’s growth story."
"We’re seeing real momentum across both stores and digital, and we want to build on that by continuing to invest in the people, infrastructure and partnerships that will support our ambitions in Ireland for the long-term."
“Our relationship with RTS has grown over eight years, and this next step means we can bring even more of our Irish operation closer to our customers. Holding more stock locally will help us deliver faster and offer greater choice and availability, while allowing us to continue investing in Ireland and building our presence in what is a very important market for us.”
Mick McConnell, Managing Director, Road Truck Services, says: "We’re incredibly proud of our partnership with Holland & Barrett, which has gone from strength to strength over the past eight years. Growing together has enabled us to expand our warehousing and transport capabilities, strengthen our business and secure other high-profile contracts."
“This latest investment marks an exciting new chapter in our relationship, creating jobs locally and allowing us to play an even bigger role in supporting Holland & Barrett’s growth in Ireland.”

items.title: Nisa Local convenience stores deploy Quail Digital headset technology to improve parcel services
items.summary: Kash Retail, which operates multiple convenience stores in the UK branded as Nisa Local, has introduced digital headsets by Quail Digital into its outlets following a six-week trial.The technology enables colleagues to communicate instantly across the shopfloor without leaving their positions or int
items.body:
Kash Retail, which operates multiple convenience stores in the UK branded as Nisa Local, has introduced digital headsets by Quail Digital into its outlets following a six-week trial.
The technology enables colleagues to communicate instantly across the shopfloor without leaving their positions or interrupting customer service’ and is helping stores manage everyday operational challenges more effectively, according to the retail operator.
Kevin Polley, Operations Manager at Kash Retail, says: “One of the clearest benefits has been the handling of parcel collections. When a customer arrives at the till to collect a parcel, the colleague serving them can contact a shopfloor team member through their headset and ask them to locate it."
“This removes the need to leave the till or call across the store, helping keep the collection process moving and reducing customer waiting times. The headsets have been a great help in speeding up the collection process, as staff on the tills can request a shopfloor colleague to find the parcel.”
Polley says the new digital headset system, called Quail Connect, is also helping the retailer respond more quickly when additional till support is required. Colleagues can request assistance directly through their headsets as queues build, allowing the team to react without leaving customers unattended. He also highlights how the technology is improving staff wellbeing by helping colleagues feel safer and better supported when dealing with potential theft and other security concerns.
Quail Connect is designed for small retail stores, typically accommodating four to six users, with the flexibility to expand as required.
Tom Downes, Founder and CEO at Quail Digital, says: “Retailers are being asked to manage an increasingly complex range of in-store services while maintaining high standards of customer service. Parcel collections are a good example of how even a seemingly straightforward task can create additional pressure on store teams if communication is slow or inefficient."
“By giving colleagues, a simple, hands free way to communicate, Quail Connect helps ensure the right person can respond quickly, whether that means locating a parcel, opening another till or alerting a colleague to a potential security concern.”

items.body:
THG Fulfil and CDS Superstores, trading as The Range, wilko and Homebase, have agreed a multi-year contract extension.
The deal builds on a partnership that began in 2024, in which THG Fulfil provides fulfilment and courier management services for the home, leisure and garden retailer.
The renewal supports CDS Superstores’ digital transformation as it looks to invest in technology to strengthen the online offer for The Range, wilko and Homebase. This includes Google Cloud AI technologies to improve search and product discovery on wilko.com, and Mirakl’s platform to support the growth of The Range’s online marketplace.
CDS Superstores is tapping THG Fulfil’s warehouse automation, with 95% of units sold passing through a form of automation during the fulfilment journey. This includes a fleet of Geekplus goods-to-person robots.
Tom Killeen, COO, THG Ingenuity, says: “We believe fulfilment is the centre of customer excellence and brand reputation, and we look forward to continuing to offer CDS Superstores a best-in-class fulfilment service experience for their customers.”
Ben Exall, Group Chief Digital & Marketing Officer, CDS Superstores (The Range, wilko & Homebase) says: “Digital transformation is central to our growth plans for The Range, wilko & Homebase. We’re investing in technology to make it easier for customers to find and shop our products online, alongside our expanding store network. Extending our partnership with THG Fulfil gives us the capacity and flexibility to support that growth, with reliable delivery that customers can depend on.”

items.title: WHSmith rolls out x-hoppers communication platform to 300+ stores after pilot
items.summary: x-hoppers, an AI powered retail communication platform from Wildix, has announced a new partnership with WHSmith following a pilot.The retailer is rolling out the platform across 300+ UK stores, starting with 32 priority locations. The first of these, its flagship location at Heathrow Terminal 5, is
items.body:
x-hoppers, an AI powered retail communication platform from Wildix, has announced a new partnership with WHSmith following a pilot.
The retailer is rolling out the platform across 300+ UK stores, starting with 32 priority locations. The first of these, its flagship location at Heathrow Terminal 5, is now live.
WHSmith selected x-hoppers to support its store teams with wireless headsets, a web app for head office and an AI powered assistant. The pilot began in late 2025 at Manchester Piccadilly station, one of WHSmith’s busiest travel locations. More than 43,000 smart notifications have been delivered to colleagues’ headsets, from store alerts and fridge and freezer monitoring to scheduled team updates and customer QR code alerts. This brings communication, alerts and requests together in one place and reduces reliance on manual processes.
In key categories, QR code notifications let customers request help on the spot, so teams can respond at the point of need. The same codes let delivery drivers contact store teams directly, minimising delays at drop-offs, and can be adapted to store-specific workflows.
Over the course of the pilot, customers made almost 1,000 requests for help via QR codes. Compared with before x-hoppers was installed, WHSmith has seen QR codes deliver a sales uplift of up to +22% in key categories.
Karl Stakes, Director of Operations at WHSmith, says: “Our colleagues need to be able to help customers quickly, especially when stores are busy. x-hoppers keeps our teams connected, so customers get help faster and colleagues are never on their own. The pilot showed what it can do, and we’re pleased to be rolling it out."
“x-hoppers was built to make retail teams more connected and effective,” says Graham Dixon, CTO at x-hoppers. “Seeing WHSmith achieve up to +22% sales uplift in the pilot and move to a roll-out across more than 300 stores shows the real, measurable value of uniting people, systems and AI on one platform.”

items.title: McKinsey research shows retailers are losing the start of the shopping journey to AI tools
items.summary: 29% of AI shoppers say AI chat or search tools had the biggest influence on their most recent purchase - three times the share citing traditional search engines (9%), and more than retailers’ platforms and AI assistants combined (21%), according to new McKinsey & Company research drawing on a su
items.body:
29% of AI shoppers say AI chat or search tools had the biggest influence on their most recent purchase - three times the share citing traditional search engines (9%), and more than retailers’ platforms and AI assistants combined (21%), according to new McKinsey & Company research drawing on a survey of approximately 21,000 consumers in 11 markets.
The shift is moving beyond discovery to influence and transactions. In the US, the share of AI users completing a purchase through AI has surged 70% since December 2025, from 10% to 17%.
Kelsey Robinson, Senior Partner, McKinsey & Company, says: "Consumers are showing unmet appetite and preference for AI shopping. Nearly a third of AI shoppers said AI chat or search tools were the biggest influence on their recent purchase. The winners this holiday season will be those that have stood up an agentic capability and are treating this as an always-on experimentation muscle."
53% of consumers across the 11 markets now use AI for shopping. China (80%) and India (76%) lead adoption, while Japan (37%) and France (44%) have the lowest shares. Despite leading in private AI investment, the US is below the average, at 48%.
Among all US adults, not just those who use AI, the share completing a purchase through AI has doubled from 5% to 9% since December 2025. Among users, the US (17%) is ahead of the global average (14%), the UK (11%), Germany (10%) and France (8%).
As the holiday season approaches, retailers are racing to enable AI powered purchases, opening their systems to authorised AI agents in a secure way. They face a new battle for shoppers as AI chat and search tools are used nearly twice as often as retailers’ own assistants for shopping inspiration (45% vs 23% of AI users respectively). But at checkout, retailers regain ground: 15% of AI users have completed a purchase using a retailer assistant, compared to 14% through a chat or search tool.
AI is also gaining ground in categories that have traditionally lagged in online shopping. E-commerce laggards such as beauty (34%) and groceries (32%), now closely trail behind consumer electronics (38%), clothing (37%) and travel (35%) as categories where AI users have turned to AI to research or decide what to buy.
In the US, 42% of users have tapped AI for grocery decisions, while the share buying groceries through AI has jumped 11 percentage points since December 2025 - the largest increase of any category measured.
Jack Trotter, Partner at McKinsey & Company, comments: “Shoppers are handing AI the legwork. They’re using it to save time, cut down their options and surface brands they hadn’t found on their own, raising the stakes for brands to be on the AI agent’s shortlist. Retailers need to be where that agent can complete the purchase. Whether that’s through product data agents can read and checkout agents can use, including their own AI shopping assistants.”
